meta.titre: Bearings: Directions, Distances and Angles of Elevation
meta.sous_theme: Three-figure bearings, back bearings, elevation and depression

sections.contenu_markdown: A pilot flying from Douala to Garoua, a captain steering a boat out of Kribi and a hiker in the Bamenda highlands all answer the same question: in which direction must I go? Compass words such as north-east are too vague, so navigators use bearings, an angle measured from north. At the GCE, bearing questions combine three skills that you already own: angle facts on parallel lines, right-angled trigonometry and the sine and cosine rules. The same questions often include angles of elevation and depression.

items: North, East, South and West are $0^\circ$ (or $360^\circ$), $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ and $270^\circ$ measured clockwise from north.
Co-interior angles between parallel lines add up to $180^\circ$.

sections.contenu_markdown:
**Definition.** The bearing of a point $B$ from a point $A$ is the angle measured **clockwise from the north line at $A$** to the line $AB$. It is always written with **three figures**: $045^\circ$, not $45^\circ$.

| Direction | N | NE | E | SE | S | SW | W | NW |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bearing | $000^\circ$ | $045^\circ$ | $090^\circ$ | $135^\circ$ | $180^\circ$ | $225^\circ$ | $270^\circ$ | $315^\circ$ |

**Method for a journey problem**

1. Draw a sketch. At every town, draw a north line pointing up.
2. Mark each bearing as a clockwise angle from the north line at the point you start from.
3. Use the fact that the north lines are parallel to turn bearings into angles inside the triangle.
4. Choose the tool: Pythagoras or $\sin$, $\cos$, $\tan$ for a right angle; the cosine rule $c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}-2ab\cos C$ when two sides and the angle between them are known; the sine rule $\dfrac{a}{\sin A}=\dfrac{b}{\sin B}$ when an angle and its opposite side are known.
5. To give a bearing, add or subtract the triangle angle to a known bearing and write three figures.

**Check.** A bearing is between $000^\circ$ and $360^\circ$. Put your calculator in degree mode.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When you know the bearing of $B$ from $A$ and need the bearing of $A$ from $B$.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Add $180^\circ$ if the bearing is less than $180^\circ$, and subtract $180^\circ$ if it is more than $180^\circ$. The north lines are parallel, so the two directions are opposite.

Example: the bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $070^\circ$, so the bearing of $A$ from $B$ is $070^\circ+180^\circ=250^\circ$. If it were $300^\circ$, the back bearing would be $300^\circ-180^\circ=120^\circ$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a person looks up at, or down from, a tower, cliff or lighthouse.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Both angles are measured from the **horizontal**. The angle of elevation is measured upward, the angle of depression downward. Because horizontal lines are parallel, the angle of depression of a boat seen from a tower equals the angle of elevation of the tower seen from the boat (alternate angles).

For a tower of height $h$ and an angle $\theta$ at the boat, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{h}{d}$, so $d=\dfrac{h}{\tan\theta}$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a bearing and distance must be split into north and east parts.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A journey of distance $d$ on a bearing $\theta$ (with $\theta$ between $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$) goes $d\cos\theta$ northward and $d\sin\theta$ eastward. For other bearings, find the acute angle with the north-south line first.

sections.enonce_markdown: A boat leaves port $P$ and sails $12$ km on a bearing of $065^\circ$ to a buoy $Q$. It then sails $9$ km on a bearing of $140^\circ$ to a rock $R$. Find (a) the distance $PR$ to $2$ decimal places and (b) the bearing of $R$ from $P$ to the nearest degree.

etapes.action: Find the angle $PQR$ inside the triangle.
etapes.justification: The bearing of $P$ from $Q$ is the back bearing $065^\circ+180^\circ=245^\circ$ (parallel north lines). The path $QR$ has bearing $140^\circ$, and the angle between $QP$ and $QR$ is the difference of the two bearings.
Two sides ($PQ=12$, $QR=9$) and the angle between them are known.
The distance is the positive root.

etapes.action: Find $\angle QPR$ with the sine rule.
etapes.justification: We now know side $QR=9$ opposite $\angle QPR$ and side $PR$ opposite the $105^\circ$ angle. Since $QR<PQ$, the angle at $P$ is acute.

etapes.action: Add to the bearing of $Q$ from $P$.
etapes.justification: Seen from $P$, the rock $R$ lies further clockwise than $Q$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: $PR=16.76$ km and the bearing of $R$ from $P$ is $096^\circ$.

items.pourquoi_faux: A bearing always has three figures. Writing two figures is marked as incorrect.

items.erreur_markdown: The bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $070^\circ$, so the bearing of $A$ from $B$ is $110^\circ$ (that is $180^\circ-70^\circ$).
items.pourquoi_faux: A back bearing is found by adding or subtracting $180^\circ$, because the bearing is measured clockwise from north at the new point.

items.erreur_markdown: Measuring the bearing anticlockwise, or from the east line.
items.pourquoi_faux: Bearings are always measured clockwise from the north line at the point you are starting from.
items.correction_markdown: Draw the north line at the starting point, then measure clockwise. For a point due west the bearing is $270^\circ$, not $90^\circ$.

items.erreur_markdown: Using $AC^{2}=AB^{2}+BC^{2}$ in a triangle with a $105^\circ$ angle at $B$.
items.pourquoi_faux: Pythagoras works only when the angle is exactly $90^\circ$. Otherwise use the cosine rule.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Write down the three-figure bearing of the directions east, south-west and north-west.

(b) The bearing of a village $V$ from a school $S$ is $125^\circ$. Find the bearing of $S$ from $V$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) East is $090^\circ$, south-west is $225^\circ$, north-west is $315^\circ$.

**Answer: $090^\circ$, $225^\circ$, $315^\circ$.**

(b) The back bearing is $125^\circ+180^\circ=305^\circ$.

**Answer: $305^\circ$.**

items.enonce_markdown: A motorcyclist rides $20$ km from Kumba on a bearing of $040^\circ$. Find, correct to $2$ decimal places, (a) how far north he has travelled, (b) how far east he has travelled, (c) the bearing of Kumba from his position.
items.solution_markdown:
The path makes an angle of $40^\circ$ with the north line, so the north-south side is adjacent to the angle and the east-west side is opposite.

(a) North: $20\cos 40^\circ=20\times 0.7660=15.32$ km.

(b) East: $20\sin 40^\circ=20\times 0.6428=12.86$ km.

(c) Back bearing: $040^\circ+180^\circ=220^\circ$.

**Answer: $15.32$ km north, $12.86$ km east, bearing $220^\circ$.**

items.enonce_markdown: The top of a lighthouse $L$ is $40$ m above sea level. From the top, the angle of depression of a boat $B_1$ lying due east of the lighthouse is $18^\circ$. A second boat $B_2$ is $90$ m due south of $B_1$. Find (a) the horizontal distance from the foot of the lighthouse to $B_1$, (b) the distance from the foot $F$ of the lighthouse to $B_2$, (c) the bearing of $B_2$ from $F$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The angle of elevation of the top from $B_1$ is also $18^\circ$, so $\tan 18^\circ=\dfrac{40}{FB_1}$ and $FB_1=\dfrac{40}{\tan 18^\circ}=123.1$ m (1 d.p.).

(b) $FB_1$ points east and $B_1B_2$ points south, so triangle $FB_1B_2$ has a right angle at $B_1$. $FB_2=\sqrt{123.1^{2}+90^{2}}=152.5$ m.

(c) In that triangle $\tan\angle B_1FB_2=\dfrac{90}{123.1}$, so $\angle B_1FB_2=36.2^\circ$. Starting from east ($090^\circ$) and turning clockwise towards south, the bearing is $090^\circ+36.2^\circ=126.2^\circ\approx 126^\circ$.

**Answer: $123.1$ m, $152.5$ m and $126^\circ$.**

items_markdown: A bearing is measured **clockwise from north** and is written with **three figures**.
Back bearing: add $180^\circ$ if the bearing is below $180^\circ$, subtract $180^\circ$ if it is above.
Always sketch, with a north line at every point; parallel north lines give the angles inside the triangle.
Right angle: Pythagoras or SOH CAH TOA. Otherwise: cosine rule (two sides and the included angle) or sine rule (angle and opposite side).
Angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the bottom; both are measured from the horizontal.
